title: India's Silver Import Crackdown Creates Shortages and Sends Premiums Soaring
excerpt: Import restrictions and a duty hike to 15% have slashed India's silver imports by more than 90%, pushing domestic premiums to six-month highs and threatening global price dynamics.
body:
• India's silver imports plunged 94% year-on-year to just 33 metric tons in May after the government restricted imports in nearly all forms and raised duties from 6% to 15%.
  • Domestic silver premiums surged to $6.50 per ounce — more than 10% above global benchmark prices — swinging from discounts of $5.50 in May.
  • The restrictions aim to narrow India's trade deficit and support the rupee, which hit a record low of 91.74 against the dollar in January 2026.
  • Analysts warn premiums could climb further as festive and wedding season demand picks up, with confusion over import licensing rules adding to supply constraints.

India's crackdown on silver imports has created acute shortages in the world's largest market for the precious metal, driving domestic premiums to their highest level in six months even as demand remains below seasonal norms.

The government moved in mid-May to restrict silver imports in nearly all forms with immediate effect. In June, it tightened rules further by adding silver grain and powder to the restricted category and requiring prior import authorisation. Combined with a sharp increase in import duties — from 6% to 15% — the measures have brought overseas silver shipments to a near halt.

The Numbers Tell the Story

Silver imports collapsed to just 33 metric tons in May, down 94% from 534.3 tons a year earlier, according to Ministry of Commerce data. In dollar terms, imports fell to $75.57 million from $566.22 million — the lowest since February 2023. Imports fell further in June, according to industry participants.

For the full year to date, India has imported 1,837 tonnes of silver, a 16% year-on-year decline and about 3% below the five-year average, according to Metals Focus data.

"Silver imports have nearly come to a halt, creating a shortage in the Indian market. As a result, silver is trading at a significant premium to global prices."

— Chirag Thakkar, CEO of Amrapali Group Gujarat

Premiums Swing From Discounts to Records

The supply squeeze has flipped the domestic pricing dynamic. Silver premiums over official prices surged to $6.50 per ounce in early July — more than 10% above benchmark levels — compared with discounts of as much as $5.50 an ounce in May, according to Reuters. While premiums have not yet matched the peaks seen during last year's silver squeeze, they are approaching those levels.

In January, gold premiums had already surged past $100 an ounce — the highest since 2014 — as traders priced in anticipated curbs. Silver premiums hit a then-record $8 per ounce before the import duty hike took effect.

Why India Is Clamping Down

The restrictions are part of a broader effort to shore up India's foreign exchange reserves and contain a widening current account deficit (CAD), which has ballooned amid elevated oil prices. Precious metals are the second-largest import category by value after crude oil, accounting for 7% to 10% of India's total merchandise imports.

India spent a record $12 billion on silver imports in the 2025/26 financial year, up from $4.8 billion the previous year. The rupee's slide to a record low of 91.74 against the dollar intensified pressure on policymakers to act.

Market Impact and Outlook

Lower imports by India — which meets more than 80% of its silver demand through overseas purchases — could weigh on global prices while helping narrow the country's trade deficit. Domestically, the market has become largely dependent on supplies from Hindustan Zinc, India's biggest silver producer.

After the May duty hike, some investors booked profits and exited silver exchange-traded funds (ETFs), briefly releasing metal into the domestic market. But those supplies have since dried up, tightening the squeeze further.

Metals Focus analysts warn the situation will likely worsen in the coming months as demand picks up during the festive wedding season. Confusion about the new import licensing requirements is further restricting flows, even for traders willing to pay the higher duties.

India imports silver primarily from the United Arab Emirates, Britain, and China. The metal is used across jewellery, coins, bars, and industrial applications including solar panels and electronics. In the past year, investment demand — particularly through silver ETFs — has overtaken traditional jewellery and silverware consumption.
